extracted.intended_audience: journal editors, publishers, peer reviewers, and research-integrity officers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for detecting submissions produced by paper mills and identifying red flags during editorial handling, correspondence, and post-publication investigation. Focus is on practical signs (emails, metadata, author responses, data availability) that suggest fraudulent, outsourced manuscripts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of commercial instead of academic email addresses
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors linked to paper mills always used commercial instead of academic email addresses; often the email addresses had little relation to the name of the corresponding author. Some authors claimed their institutions do not provide academic addresses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seifert concluded the lack of academic email addresses renders identification of fraudulent authors much more difficult and that all real academic institutions provide academic email addresses. As a policy response, the journal no longer allows submissions without a valid academic (or pharmaceutical company) email address. Note trade-offs: some legitimate authors lack functional institutional email access in certain regions or circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Puzzling email clusters / near-identical correspondence
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors received emails from authors from apparently different groups within a short period (minutes to hours) with rather similar text, suggesting one person using multiple addresses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat strikingly similar or clustered correspondence as a red flag for a single paper-mill employee handling multiple fake submissions in one session. Compare wording across submissions and track timing patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sluggish or non-responsive email communication
rubrics_metrics.description: Sometimes there was no communication at all, or responses took up to six months; authors cited servers blocking messages as excuses though editors rarely received delivery failure notices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long, evasive, or nonexistent correspondence from corresponding authors (especially after queries about data or authorship) is a warning sign. This sluggishness contributed to slow retraction processes; consider policies (e.g., response deadlines) to avoid delay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invalid or non-working co-author email addresses
rubrics_metrics.description: Email addresses — especially of co-authors — did not work or were invalid; authors sometimes claimed server blocking as an excuse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check co-author email validity as part of screening; non-functioning co-author addresses (or addresses that bounce) are suspicious. Manual checks of institutional affiliation and email can help identify fraud.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence or paucity of ORCID IDs
rubrics_metrics.description: Very few authors used ORCID IDs in the cases studied; this can disguise identity, especially where names are common.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Low ORCID uptake among authors may be a red flag, though ORCID is not an identity verification system and can be gamed. Use ORCID presence as one indicator among others rather than definitive proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rapid agreement to retract without admitting fraud
rubrics_metrics.description: When confronted, corresponding authors often very quickly (within hours and almost simultaneously) agreed to a retraction, using vague language like 'problem with the data' without specific admission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fast, non-defensive agreement to retract (combined with vague explanations) can indicate paper-mill involvement; contrast quick assent with later evasiveness over formal retraction steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Painful, formal retraction process exploited by mills
rubrics_metrics.description: The formal retraction process was sluggish on the authors' side and lacked professional conduct; paper mills exploit COPE/formal rules to delay retraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should be aware that existing retraction procedures can be gamed. Consider policy changes such as tighter time limits for author responses, requirements to supply raw data within deadlines, or processes that allow retraction when clear evidence exists without prolonged author cooperation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requesting original/raw data at submission as a prevention measure
rubrics_metrics.description: Requesting original data at submission was suggested as a prevention method and to improve reproducibility, though concern exists that paper mills might start selling fabricated 'raw' data as part of their package.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requiring submission of raw data or primary images can deter some fraud and aid verification. Be aware of the arms race risk: mills may adapt and provide fabricated data. Editorial workflows and reviewer expectations may need strengthening to assess legitimacy of supplied data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of compiled evidence (spreadsheets, metadata) to detect patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: Excel/Google spreadsheets compiling suspected papers helped bring problems to editors' attention and were useful in nailing down fraud.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain structured records of suspicious submissions (metadata, shared phrases, timelines, email addresses) to identify patterns across manuscripts. Collaborative tracking tools can reveal clusters from the same mill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suspicious topical/title patterns and formulaic subject combinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Commenters noted that certain title/term combinations (e.g., 'axis' plus multiple hot RNA terms like 'miRNA', 'lncRNA', 'circRNA') can indicate likely bogus papers or mill-produced content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be alert for formulaic, buzzword-stuffed titles or repetitive combinations of trendy terms across submissions. Topic-pattern heuristics can flag manuscripts for closer scrutiny but must be used carefully to avoid unfairly disadvantaging legitimate work in certain subfields.
